title: Vasquez’s standing ‘perhaps otherwise’ judgment cancels even conjectural certainty
source_text: L. Si vero dicatur aliqua formido deceptionis nunquam abesse a certitudine quam fideles habent de sua justitia, quia cum illa semper stat judicium istud, Fortasse oppositum in re est, &, Forte res habet aliter quam opinor, prout formidinem illam exponit Vasquez; dicimus tale judicium pugnare cum quacunque certitudine quae veri nominis sit, non excepta morali, sive conjecturali. Etenim omnis certitudo, etiam moralis, sive conjecturalis, excludit fluctuationem & haesitationem, fatentibus ipsis Scholae Romanae Doctoribus, nec reperitur, nisi in assensu fixo & determinato, quorum ita se habere judicamus. Qui vero opinans atque conjiciens quod res eo modo se habet, nihilominus judicat fortasse eam aliter se habere, non caret hac in parte haesitatione, & fluctuatione; & licet ad unam partem magis inclinet, non tamen habet ad eam assensum fixum atque determinatum, ac proinde non habet, vel minimum illum certitudinis gradum, qui reperitur in certitudine quam conjecturalem appellant. Conjicit ergo ille, suspicatur atque opinatur, nullo vero modo certus est. Cum enim aliquis certo colligit & statuit, ex variis signis atque indiciis, rem sic, vel secus, se habere, ut, exempli gratia, hunc & illum aegrotum hydrope, vel phthisi laborare; hanc epistolam, ab eo amico, vel cognato, missam vel scriptam esse; non amplius apud se dicit, Fortasse non ita est, sed, Proculdubio res eo modo se habet, nec ratiocinatur in judicando eam aliter se habere: quamvis simul judicet, absolute loquendo, non impossibile esse, ut sese aliter habeat.
pass_a_gloss: But if it be said that some fear of deception never is absent from the certainty which the faithful have concerning their righteousness, because with it there always stands that judgment, Perhaps the opposite is in the matter, and, Perhaps the matter stands otherwise than I think, as Vasquez explains that fear: we say that such a judgment fights with whatever certainty is of true name, not excepting the moral or conjectural. For every certainty, even moral or conjectural, excludes fluctuation and hesitation, the doctors of the Roman School themselves confessing, and is not found except in a fixed and determinate assent of those things which we judge so to stand. But he who, opining and conjecturing that the matter stands in that way, nevertheless judges that perhaps it stands otherwise, is not without hesitation and fluctuation in this part; and although he inclines more to one part, yet he does not have toward it a fixed and determinate assent, and therefore does not have even that least grade of certainty which is found in the certainty they call conjectural. He therefore conjectures, suspects, and opines; but in no way is he certain. For when someone certainly gathers and determines from various signs and indications that the matter stands thus or otherwise—as, for example, that this or that sick person labors with dropsy or consumption; that this letter was sent or written by that friend or kinsman—he no longer says within himself, Perhaps it is not so, but, Doubtless the matter stands in that way, nor does he reason in judging that it stands otherwise: although at the same time he judges, speaking absolutely, that it is not impossible that it stand otherwise.
pass_b_english: A live ‘perhaps I’m wrong’ veto is incompatible even with conjectural certainty.
Ordinary moral certainty says ‘doubtless thus,’ while still admitting absolute possibility otherwise.
